Non-Invertible Symmetries on Tensor-Product Hilbert Spaces and Quantum Cellular Automata
Rui Wen, Kansei Inamura, Sakura Schäfer-Nameki, [0.4em] Mathematical Institute, University of OxfordAndrew Wiles Building, Woodstock Road, Oxford, OX2 6GG, UK

Abstract
We investigate realizations of ( 1 + 1 ) (1+1) -dimensional fusion category symmetries on tensor-product Hilbert spaces, allowing for mixing with quantum cellular automata (QCAs). It was argued recently that any such realizable symmetry must be weakly integral. We develop a systematic analysis of QCA-refined realizations of fusion categories and prove two statements. First, we show that, under certain physical assumptions on defects, any QCA-refined realization has QCA and symmetry-operator indices determined by the categorical data, up to the freedom of redefining the symmetry operators. Second, we construct a lattice model that provides a QCA-refined realization for any weakly integral fusion category symmetry on a tensor product Hilbert space. We also compute indices of the QCAs in our lattice model and show agreement with the first result. As an application of the general construction, we give an explicit QCA-refined realization of general Tambara-Yamagami categorical symmetries.

Introduction and Summary

The modern understanding of symmetries in quantum
many-body systems and quantum field theory has expanded well beyond the traditional setting of groups. In the continuum, it is expected that a finite generalized internal symmetry in spacetime dimension
(1+1)
D is described by a unitary fusion category

This has led to the construction of new gapped phases and phase-transitions with fusion categorical symmetries using various continuum field theory and categorical methods

On the other hand lattice model realizations of categorical symmetries are more subtle. Although applicable to any fusion category, the anyon chain in
(1+1)
D realizes these symmetries at the cost of not necessarily having a tensor-product Hilbert space structure

A natural question is then which categorical symmetries can be realized on a tensor-product Hilbert space
1
1

1

We always assume the on-site Hilbert space is finite dimensional.
. There are two separate cases to consider. First is when the symmetry is realized strictly on the Hilbert space. This means the symmetry operators form a representation of the fusion rules. It has been proven recently in
[
42
]
that a fusion categorical symmetry can be realized strictly on a tensor-product Hilbert space if and only if it is
integral
. A fusion category is called integral if all objects have integral quantum dimension.
The second case, which is the focus of this paper, is when the symmetry is realized by mixing with quantum cellular automata (QCAs). In this paper, QCAs mean unitary operators that map local operators to nearby local operators. Prototypical examples of QCAs include lattice translations and finite-depth quantum circuits. See
[
43
,
44
]
for reviews on this subject.

It has been observed in many models that it is possible to realize non-integral fusion categorical symmetries on a tensor-product Hilbert space if we allow mixing with QCAs
[
45
,
46
,
47
,
48
,
49
,
50
]
. A basic example is the Ising fusion category. Specifically, on a spin chain with on-site Hilbert space dimension 2, it is possible to construct symmetry operators
\mathsf{D}_{f},\mathsf{D}_{\sigma}
that satisfy the following product rule
[
46
,
45
]

\mathsf{D}_{f}\mathsf{D}_{f}=1,~\mathsf{D}_{f}\mathsf{D}_{\sigma}=\mathsf{D}_{\sigma}\mathsf{D}_{f}=\mathsf{D}_{\sigma},~\mathsf{D}_{\sigma}\mathsf{D}_{\sigma}=T(1+\mathsf{D}_{f})~,

(1.1)

where
T
is lattice translation by a site. We recover the Ising category fusion rules by setting
T
to identity. In the IR of any system with the above symmetry, it is expected that lattice translation will flow to the trivial operator and the symmetry reduces to a
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
-Tambara Yamagami category (i.e.
\mathrm{TY}(\mathbb{Z}_{2},+)
or
\mathrm{TY}(\mathbb{Z}_{2},-)

[
45
]
).
The appearance of lattice translation in the product rule
Equation

1.1
is what we mean by mixing with QCAs. The lattice translation operator
T
is a non-trivial QCA. Other examples of this type were studied in
[
47
]
. In general, a fusion category
\mathcal{C}
is realized on a tensor-product Hilbert space up to QCAs if the symmetry operators
\mathsf{D}_{x},x\in\mathcal{C}
satisfy a modified product rule

\mathsf{D}_{x}\mathsf{D}_{y}=\sum_{z\in\mathcal{C}}U^{z}_{xy}\mathsf{D}_{z}\,,

(1.2)

where
U^{z}_{xy}
are QCAs, such that the fusion rules of
\mathcal{C}
is recovered by setting all QCAs to identity. We will call a realization of a fusion categorical symmetry in the form of
Equation

1.2
a
QCA-refined realization
, and
Equation

1.2
the
QCA-refined fusion rules
.

The weak integrality conjecture
[
47
,
51
,
52
]
states that a fusion categorical symmetry admitting a QCA-refined realization on a tensor-product Hilbert space must be
weakly integral
. A fusion category is called weakly integral if its total quantum dimension is an integer, or equivalently, if the square of the quantum dimension of any simple object is an integer. Evidence for this conjecture is emerging, including a recent conditional proof in
[
51
]
and a proof for the case of duality operators in
[
53
]
. See also
[
54
]
for a related discussion.

In this paper we are concerned with the following two questions.

Question 1
.

Assuming a fusion categorical symmetry
\mathcal{C}
is realized on a tensor-product Hilbert space as in
Equation

1.2
, what are the constraints on the QCAs
U^{z}_{xy}
imposed by the categorical data of
\mathcal{C}
?

Question 2
.

The converse to the weak integrality conjecture: Is it true that every weakly integral fusion category admits a QCA-refined realization on a tensor-product Hilbert space?

Our main results are complete answers to these two questions.

Result 1
.

Under certain physical assumptions about topological defects of symmetries, we prove the following: If a fusion categorical symmetry
\mathcal{C}
admits a QCA-refined realization as in
Equation

1.2
, then the Gross-Nesme-Vogts-Werner (GNVW) indices
[
55
]
of the QCAs
U^{z}_{xy}
are uniquely determined by
\mathcal{C}
up to redefinition of symmetry operators.

The assumptions are detailed in
Section

2.1
.
Here, by redefinition of symmetry operators, we allow for adding ancilla and redefining
\mathsf{D}_{x}\mapsto\alpha_{x}\mathsf{D}_{x}
where
\alpha_{x}
is a QCA. Two QCA-refined realizations of the same fusion category related by such a redefinition should be considered as being equivalent, similar to equivalence between projective representations of groups.

Result 2
.

We construct a lattice model that realizes any weakly integral fusion categorical symmetry on a tensor-product Hilbert space, up to QCAs. Therefore we have the following.

Theorem 1.1
.

Any weakly integral fusion categorical symmetry admits a QCA-refined realization on a tensor-product Hilbert space.

We will compute the GNVW indices of the QCAs
U^{z}_{xy}
in our lattice model and confirm that they agree with the prediction of our
Result

1
. We will also compute the generalized GNVW indices for the symmetry operators
\mathsf{D}_{x}
following the definition of the generalized GNVW index in
[
51
]
. These calculations provide a consistency check on the physical assumptions needed for
Result

1
. Applying the general construction, we obtain an explicit tensor-product realization of general Tambara-Yamagami fusion categories up to translation, which has not been achieved in existing literature.

We stress that the weak integrality conjecture, in its full general form, remains open. The proof given in
[
51
]
, which we will review in
Section

2.2
, relies on certain physically well-motivated assumptions that should ultimately be derived from first principles. One possible route towards a proof is to justify the physical assumptions, starting with a proper definition of the symmetry operator. It may be that the upcoming work
[
56
]
will elucidate this point. This combined with the results of the present paper could then provide us an "if and only if" statement about realizability of non-invertible symmetries on tensor-product Hilbert spaces up to QCAs.

2.1
Physical Assumptions and Consequences

We now review the physical assumptions about topological defects of symmetry operators that are needed for our
Result

1
. Although we do not prove these, the

1
to
5
are satisfied by common realization of well-studied symmetries, including group-theoretical symmetries, non-anomalous symmetries, and Kramers-Wannier duality symmetry
[
51
]
.
We consider a spin chain with tensor-product Hilbert space

\mathcal{H}=\bigotimes_{i=1}^{L}h^{(i)}\,,

(2.1)

where
L
is the length of the chain and
h^{(i)}
is the local Hilbert space on site
i
. We assume that
h^{(i)}
is finite dimensional and independent of
i
up to isomorphism, that is,
h^{(i)}\simeq h
for some finite dimensional Hilbert space
h\simeq\mathbb{C}^{d}
. Then
d
is called the on-site dimension. Let
\{\mathsf{D}_{x}\}
be a collection of possibly non-invertible symmetry operators acting on
\mathcal{H}
.

Assumption 1
.

For every symmetry operator
\mathsf{D}_{x}
, we assume that there are corresponding left and right defect Hilbert spaces
\mathcal{H}_{x}^{l}
and
\mathcal{H}_{x}^{r}
, which are obtained by modifying the original Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}
in a finite region:

\mathcal{H}_{\mathsf{D}_{x}}^{l}=\left(\bigotimes_{i\in\{1,\cdots,L\}-I_{x}}h^{(i)}\right)\otimes L_{x},\hskip 20.00003pt\mathcal{H}_{\mathsf{D}_{x}}^{r}=\left(\bigotimes_{i\in\{1,\cdots,L\}-J_{x}}h^{(i)}\right)\otimes R_{x}.

(2.2)

Here,
I_{x}
and
J_{x}
are finite intervals and
L_{x}
and
R_{x}
are finite dimensional Hilbert spaces, all of which are independent of the system size
L
. In other words, the defect Hilbert spaces are obtained by replacing the Hilbert space on a finite region by a new Hilbert space. Physically, the left (right) defect Hilbert space is the Hilbert space in the presence of a defect
x
oriented upwards (downwards). We assume that the defect
x
can be moved by local unitary
operators.
2
2

2

A defect being oriented upwards (downwards) means that moving the defect to the right (left) around the chain implements the symmetry action of the corresponding operator
\mathsf{D}_{x}
. More precisely, to obtain the full symmetry action, we need to compose the unitary movement operators with the defect creation and annihilation operators, which make the symmetry operator non-invertible in general
[
58
]
.
In particular, the defect Hilbert spaces do not depend on the position of a defect up to
isomorphism.

Assumption 2
.

If
\mathsf{D}_{x}
and
\mathsf{D}_{y}
are symmetry operators, then so is
\mathsf{D}_{x}\mathsf{D}_{y}
. The defect Hilbert spaces for
\mathsf{D}_{x}\mathsf{D}_{y}
are isomorphic to the Hilbert spaces in the presence of two defects
x
and
y
apart from each other. More concretely, we assume that there are isomorphisms

\mathcal{H}_{\mathsf{D}_{x}\mathsf{D}_{y}}^{l}\simeq\left(\bigotimes_{i\in\{1,\cdots,L\}-I_{x}-I_{y}}h^{(i)}\right)\otimes L_{x}\otimes L_{y},\hskip 10.00002pt\mathcal{H}_{\mathsf{D}_{x}\mathsf{D}_{y}}^{r}\simeq\left(\bigotimes_{i\in\{1,\cdots,L\}-J_{x}-J_{y}}h^{(i)}\right)\otimes R_{x}\otimes R_{y},

(2.3)

where the overlaps
I_{x}\cap I_{y}
and
J_{x}\cap J_{y}
are empty.

Assumption 3
.

If
\mathsf{D}_{x}
and
\mathsf{D}_{y}
are symmetry operators, then so is
\mathsf{D}_{x}+\mathsf{D}_{y}
. We assume that there are isomorphisms

\mathcal{H}^{l}_{\mathsf{D}_{x}+\mathsf{D}_{y}}\simeq\mathcal{H}^{l}_{\mathsf{D}_{x}}\oplus\mathcal{H}^{l}_{\mathsf{D}_{y}},\hskip 20.00003pt\mathcal{H}^{r}_{\mathsf{D}_{x}+\mathsf{D}_{y}}\simeq\mathcal{H}^{r}_{\mathsf{D}_{x}}\oplus\mathcal{H}^{r}_{\mathsf{D}_{y}}.

(2.4)

Assumption 4
.

If
\mathsf{D}_{x}
is a symmetry operator, then so is its Hermitian conjugate
\mathsf{D}_{x}^{\dagger}
. We assume that there are isomorphisms

\mathcal{H}^{l}_{\mathsf{D}_{x}^{\dagger}}\simeq\mathcal{H}^{r}_{\mathsf{D}_{x}},\hskip 20.00003pt\mathcal{H}^{r}_{\mathsf{D}_{x}^{\dagger}}\simeq\mathcal{H}_{\mathsf{D}_{x}}^{l}.

(2.5)

For each symmetry operator
\mathsf{D}_{x}
, we define its left and right dimensions by

\mathrm{ldim}(\mathsf{D}_{x})\coloneq\frac{\dim(\mathcal{H}_{\mathsf{D}_{x}}^{l})}{\dim(\mathcal{H})},\hskip 20.00003pt\mathrm{rdim}(\mathsf{D}_{x})\coloneq\frac{\dim(\mathcal{H}_{\mathsf{D}_{x}}^{r})}{\dim(\mathcal{H})}.

(2.6)

Our
2
and
3
lead to the relations

\mathrm{ldim}(\mathsf{D}_{x}\mathsf{D}_{y})=\mathrm{ldim}(\mathsf{D}_{x})\mathrm{ldim}(\mathsf{D}_{y}),\hskip 20.00003pt\mathrm{ldim}(\mathsf{D}_{x}+\mathsf{D}_{y})=\mathrm{ldim}(\mathsf{D}_{x})+\mathrm{ldim}(\mathsf{D}_{y}),

(2.7)

and similarly for
\mathrm{rdim}
. This implies that
\mathrm{ldim}
and
\mathrm{rdim}
define
\mathbb{Q}^{>0}
-representations of the algebra of symmetry operators. If
U
is an invertible symmetry operator, then we have
UU^{\dagger}=1
, which combined with
4
gives

\mathrm{ldim}(U)\mathrm{rdim}(U)=1.

(2.8)

For example, if
U
is a lattice translation by one site to the right, then
\mathrm{ldim}(U)=\dim(h)
and
\mathrm{rdim}(U)=\dim(h)^{-1}

[
59
,
45
]
.

Next we define the lattice quantum dimension
\mathrm{qdim_{lat}}
and the index
\mathrm{ind}
of symmetry operators by

\mathrm{qdim_{lat}}(\mathsf{D}_{x})\coloneq\sqrt{\mathrm{ldim}(\mathsf{D}_{x})\mathrm{rdim}(\mathsf{D}_{x})},\hskip 20.00003pt\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{x})\coloneq\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{ldim}(\mathsf{D}_{x})}{\mathrm{rdim}(\mathsf{D}_{x})}}.

(2.9)

Due to the multiplicativity of the left and right dimensions, the lattice quantum dimension and index are also multiplicative:

\displaystyle\mathrm{qdim_{lat}}(\mathsf{D}_{x}\mathsf{D}_{y})

\displaystyle=\mathrm{qdim_{lat}}(\mathsf{D}_{x})\mathrm{qdim_{lat}}(\mathsf{D}_{y}),

(2.10)

\displaystyle\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{x}\mathsf{D}_{y})

\displaystyle=\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{x})\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{y}).

(2.11)

For an invertible symmetry operator
U
, we have
\mathrm{qdim_{lat}}(U)=1
and
\mathrm{ind}(U)=\mathrm{ldim}(U)
. For example, for a lattice translation by one site
T
, we have
\mathrm{ind}(T)=\dim(h)
. For a general QCA, the index defined above agrees with the Gross-Nesme-Vogts-Werner (GNVW) index defined in
[
55
]
, so our index can be thought of as a generalization of the GNVW index to non-invertible symmetries
[
51
]
.

Finally, we have the following assumption about the index.

Assumption 5
.

[Homogeneity of the index] Let
\mathsf{D}_{x}
and
\mathsf{D}_{y}
be indecomposable symmetry operators that obey the fusion rules
\mathsf{D}_{x}\mathsf{D}_{y}=\sum_{z}\mathsf{D}_{z}
, where
\mathsf{D}_{z}
s are also indecomposable. Then,
\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{z})=\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{w})
for all
\mathsf{D}_{z}
and
\mathsf{D}_{w}
that appear in the sum.

We note here that the above condition is equivalent to that
\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{z})=\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{x}\mathsf{D}_{y})
for all
\mathsf{D}_{z}
that appear in the sum. The proof can be found in
[
51
]
.

2.2
Physical Proof of the Weak Integrality Conjecture

The above physical assumptions imply the weak integrality conjecture: any fusion category
\mathcal{C}
that is realized on a tensor-product Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}
up to QCAs must be weakly integral. Here we review the proof given in
[
51
]
. We start with the following definition.

Definition 2.1
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a unitary fusion category. A
QCA-refined realization of
\mathcal{C}
is

•

A tensor-product Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}
;

•

A collection of symmetry operators
3
3

3

For our purpose the precise definition of a symmetry operator is irrelevant. Although a proper definition will be important for justifying the physical assumptions made earlier. One possible definition is as a quantum channel acting on local operators on
\mathcal{H}
with bounded spread, but it is not known if the physical assumptions will follow directly from this definition. We direct the reader to
[
60
,
42
]
for more details of this formulation of symmetry operator.

\{\mathsf{D}_{x}:x\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C})\}
on
\mathcal{H}
;

•

Such that

\mathsf{D}_{x}\mathsf{D}_{y}=\sum_{z}U^{z}_{xy}\mathsf{D}_{z}

(2.12)

where
U^{z}_{xy}
is a QCA and the sum is over simple objects as well as fusion channels;

•

The fusion rules of
\mathcal{C}
are recovered by setting
U^{z}_{xy}
to identity in
Equation

2.12
.

We refer to
Equation

2.12
as the
QCA-refined fusion rules
of
\mathcal{C}
, to distinguish them from the fusion rules of
\mathcal{C}
.
In
(1+1)
D.
Then by applying
\mathrm{ldim}(-)
to both sides of
Equation

2.12
, we obtain

\displaystyle\mathrm{ldim}(\mathsf{D}_{x})\mathrm{ldim}(\mathsf{D}_{y})=\sum_{z}\mathrm{ldim}(U^{z}_{xy})\mathrm{ldim}(\mathsf{D}_{z})

(2.13)

\displaystyle\Rightarrow

\displaystyle\mathrm{qdim_{lat}}(\mathsf{D}_{x})\mathrm{qdim_{lat}}(\mathsf{D}_{y})\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{x})\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{y})=\sum_{z}\mathrm{qdim_{lat}}(\mathsf{D}_{z})\mathrm{ind}(U^{z}_{xy}\mathsf{D}_{z})

\displaystyle\Rightarrow

\displaystyle\mathrm{qdim_{lat}}(\mathsf{D}_{x})\mathrm{qdim_{lat}}(\mathsf{D}_{y})=\sum_{z}\mathrm{qdim_{lat}}(\mathsf{D}_{z})

In the first step we used that facts that
\mathrm{ldim}=\mathrm{qdim_{lat}}\cdot\mathrm{ind}
and QCAs have trivial
\mathrm{qdim_{lat}}
. In the second step we used the homogeneity of index. Therefore
\mathrm{qdim_{lat}}(-)
defines a one dimensional representation of the fusion rules. It is known that one dimensional representation of the fusion rules is unique and is given by the quantum dimension
\dim_{\mathcal{C}}(-)

[
61
]
. We conclude that
\mathrm{qdim_{lat}}(\mathsf{D}_{x})=\dim_{\mathcal{C}}(x)
. By definition
\mathrm{qdim_{lat}}(\mathsf{D}_{x})
is a square root of a rational number, which means
\dim_{\mathcal{C}}(x)^{2}
is now a rational number. In any fusion category, the quantum dimension of any object is an algebraic integer
[
61
]
. Therefore
\dim_{\mathcal{C}}(x)^{2}=\dim_{\mathcal{C}}(x\otimes x)
is a rational algebraic integer. Any rational algebraic integer is an integer. We conclude
\dim_{\mathcal{C}}(x)^{2}
is an integer for any simple
x\in\mathcal{C}
. This is exactly the condition that
\mathcal{C}
is weakly integral.
To clarify, there are two definitions of weakly integrality. One is that the total quantum dimension
\dim(\mathcal{C})=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{C}}\dim_{\mathcal{C}}(x)^{2}
is an integer, another is that
\dim_{\mathcal{C}}(x)^{2}
is an integer for every simple object
x\in\mathcal{C}
. It turns out these two definitions are equivalent
[
61
]
.

2.3
Weakly Integral Fusion Categories

Before we move on to prove
Result

1
, we need to review some basic facts about weakly integral fusion categories. The key structural result we need about weakly integral fusion categories is summarized by the following Proposition, which is adapted from Proposition 3.5.7 of
[
61
]
.

Proposition 2.1

(
[
61
]
Proposition 3.5.7)
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a weakly integral fusion category. Then there is a group
E\simeq\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{r}
and a set of distinct square-free positive integers
n_{g},g\in E
, with
n_{0}=1
, such that there is faithful
E
-grading
\mathcal{C}=\oplus_{g}\mathcal{C}_{g}
and
d_{x}=a_{x}\sqrt{n_{g}},~\forall x\in\mathcal{C}_{g}
, with
a_{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{>0}
. Furthermore for any
g,h\in E
,
q(g,h):=\sqrt{\frac{n_{g}n_{h}}{n_{gh}}}\in\mathbb{Z}^{>0}
.

In other words, in a weakly integral fusion category
\mathcal{C}
, the quantum dimension of a simple object
d_{x}
is the product of an integral part
a_{x}
and a square-root part
\sqrt{n_{x}}
, and the square-root part of quantum dimension defines a grading: if
z
is contained in the fusion outcome of
x\otimes y
, then
\sqrt{n_{x}}\sqrt{n_{y}}=\sqrt{n_{z}}
up to rational numbers. The trivial component
\mathcal{C}_{0}
is spanned by simple objects with integral quantum dimension and is called the integral subcategory.
Let us look at some examples.

Example 2.1
.

Let
A
be an abelian group and
\mathrm{TY}(A)
be a Tambara-Yamagami category
[
62
]
. Then we have
\mathrm{TY}(A)=\mathbf{Vec}_{A}\oplus\mathbf{Vec}
. Denote the non-invertible simple as
D
, we have
d_{D}=\sqrt{|A|}
. If
|A|
is a perfect square (e.g.
A=\mathbb{Z}_{4},\,\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{2}
), then
d_{D}\in\mathbb{Z}
and
\mathrm{TY}(A)
is an integral fusion category. If
|A|
is not a perfect square, then we have two component
\mathcal{C}_{0}=\mathbf{Vec}_{A}
and
\mathcal{C}_{1}=\mathbf{Vec}
. E.g., for any prime
p
and
A=\mathbb{Z}_{p}
we have
n_{1}=p
and
q(1,1)=p
. We will discuss these fusion categories, QCA-refinement and their lattice realization in
Section

5
.

Example 2.2
.

The Metaplectic fusion categories
SO(M)_{2}
are weakly integral for any positive integer
M
. Such a fusion category is integral precisely when
M
is an odd perfect square or
M
is even and
M/2
is a perfect square. Let us consider a simple case
SO(3)_{2}
. It has simple objects

\mathbbm{1},Z,Y,X,X^{\prime}

(2.14)

with quantum dimensions

d_{\mathbbm{1}}=d_{Z}=1,\hskip 20.00003ptd_{Y}=2,\hskip 20.00003ptd_{X}=d_{X^{\prime}}=\sqrt{3}.

(2.15)

Hence
SO(3)_{2}
is weakly integral but not integral. The corresponding grading group is
E=\mathbb{Z}_{2}
, with

\mathcal{C}_{0}=\langle\mathbbm{1},Y,Z\rangle,\hskip 20.00003pt\mathcal{C}_{1}=\langle X,X^{\prime}\rangle.

(2.16)

Thus the integral fusion subcategory is
\mathcal{C}_{0}
, and for the nontrivial element
1\in\mathbb{Z}_{2}
we have

n_{1}=3,\hskip 20.00003ptq(1,1)=\sqrt{\frac{n_{1}^{2}}{n_{0}}}=3.

(2.17)

The fusion rules are

\displaystyle Z\otimes Z

\displaystyle\cong\mathbbm{1},

\displaystyle Z\otimes X

\displaystyle\cong X^{\prime},\hskip 20.00003ptZ\otimes Y\cong Y,\hskip 20.00003ptZ\otimes X^{\prime}\cong X,

\displaystyle X\otimes X

\displaystyle\cong\mathbbm{1}\oplus Y,\hskip 20.00003ptX\otimes Y\cong X\oplus X^{\prime},\hskip 20.00003ptX\otimes X^{\prime}\cong Y\oplus Z,

\displaystyle Y\otimes Y

\displaystyle\cong\mathbbm{1}\oplus Y\oplus Z,\hskip 20.00003ptY\otimes X^{\prime}\cong X\oplus X^{\prime},\hskip 20.00003ptX^{\prime}\otimes X^{\prime}\cong\mathbbm{1}\oplus Y.

One checks that these fusion rules agree with the
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
-grading. Moreover,
\mathcal{C}_{0}
is equivalent as a fusion category to
\mathbf{Rep}(S_{3})
. Indeed, the simple objects of
\mathcal{C}_{0}
satisfy

Z\otimes Z\cong\mathbbm{1},\hskip 20.00003ptZ\otimes Y\cong Y,\hskip 20.00003ptY\otimes Y\cong\mathbbm{1}\oplus Z\oplus Y,

(2.18)

which are exactly the fusion rules of the simple representations of
S_{3}
. We will discuss general Metaplectic categories and their QCA-refined realizations in more details in
Section

2.5
.

2.4
Constraints on Indices

We are now ready to prove
Result

1
. We present it here as the following theorem.

Theorem 2.1
.

Let
\mathcal{C}=\oplus_{g}\mathcal{C}_{g}
be a weakly integral fusion category as in
Proposition

2.1
. If it has a QCA-refined realization

\mathsf{D}_{x}\mathsf{D}_{y}=\sum_{z}U^{z}_{xy}\mathsf{D}_{z}

(2.19)

satisfying
1
to
5
,
then for
x\in\mathcal{C}_{g},y\in\mathcal{C}_{h}
we have

\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{x})=m_{x}\sqrt{n_{g}},\hskip 10.00002pt\mathrm{ind}(U^{z}_{xy})=\frac{m_{x}m_{y}}{m_{z}}q(g,h)=\frac{m_{x}m_{y}}{m_{z}}\sqrt{\frac{n_{g}n_{h}}{n_{gh}}},

(2.20)

for some
\{m_{x}\in\mathbb{Q}^{>0}:x\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C})\}
not determined by
\mathcal{C}
.

Notice that if we redefine symmetry operators by attaching with QCAs:
\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x}:=U_{r_{x}}\mathsf{D}_{x}
, for some QCA
U_{r_{x}}
that commutes with symmetry operators and has index
r_{x}
, then the redefined symmetry operators and the associated QCAs
\widetilde{U}^{z}_{xy}
satisfy

\mathrm{ind}(\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x})=m_{x}r_{x}\sqrt{n_{g}},\hskip 10.00002pt\mathrm{ind}(\widetilde{U}^{z}_{xy})=\frac{m_{x}r_{x}m_{y}r_{y}}{m_{z}r_{z}}\sqrt{\frac{n_{g}n_{h}}{n_{gh}}}.

(2.21)

Thus up to redefinition of symmetry operators in the above sense, the indices
\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{x}),\mathrm{ind}(U^{z}_{xy})
are completely determined by the weakly integral fusion category. For instance, we can stack with another spin chain with on-site dimension
\mathrm{lcm}(\{m_{x},x\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C})\})
, and take
U_{r_{x}}=U_{m_{x}^{-1}}
to be QCAs that only act on the stacked spin chain, then we can set
\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{x})=\sqrt{n_{g}},~\mathrm{ind}(U^{z}_{xy})=q(g,h)
, both of which are now determined by
\mathcal{C}
.

Proof.

From the proof of the weak integrality conjecture in
Section

2.2
we know that
\mathrm{qdim_{lat}}(\mathsf{D}_{x})=d_{x}
. Thus
\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{x})=\frac{\mathrm{qdim_{lat}}(\mathsf{D}_{x})}{\mathrm{rdim}(\mathsf{D}_{x})}=\frac{d_{x}}{\mathrm{rdim}(\mathsf{D}_{x})}
. Let
x\in\mathcal{C}_{g},y\in\mathcal{C}_{h},z\in\mathcal{C}_{gh}
be simple objects, we can write

d_{x}=a_{x}\sqrt{n_{g}},~d_{y}=a_{y}\sqrt{n_{h}},~d_{z}=a_{z}\sqrt{n_{gh}}.

(2.22)

By homogeneity of index we have

\mathrm{ind}(U^{z}_{xy})=\frac{\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{x})\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{y})}{\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{z})}=\frac{\mathrm{rdim}(\mathsf{D}_{z})}{\mathrm{rdim}(\mathsf{D}_{x})\mathrm{rdim}(\mathsf{D}_{y})}\frac{d_{x}d_{y}}{d_{z}}=\frac{m_{x}m_{y}}{m_{z}}\sqrt{\frac{n_{g}n_{h}}{n_{gh}}}

(2.23)

where we defined
m_{x}:=\frac{a_{x}}{\mathrm{rdim}(\mathsf{D}_{x})}\in\mathbb{Q}^{>0}
.∎

In fact, we can ask for more. The lattice model that we will construct later satisfies the property that the QCAs
U^{z}_{xy}
with the same index are in fact the same QCA. This together with the redefinition of symmetry operator trick discussed above implies that there exists a QCA-refined realization of the form

\mathsf{D}_{x}\mathsf{D}_{y}=U_{q(g,h)}\sum_{z}\mathsf{D}_{z},\hskip 10.00002ptx\in\mathcal{C}_{g},y\in\mathcal{C}_{h},

(2.24)

where
U_{q(g,h)}
is a QCA with index
q(g,h)
. Let us make this into a definition.

Definition 2.2
.

A QCA-refined realization of a weakly integral categorical symmetry is called
canonical
if it takes the form
Equation

2.24
.

Corollary 2.1
.

For every weakly integral fusion category, a canonical QCA-refined realization exists. ∎

2.5
Examples of QCA-Refined Fusion Rules

Here we consider two families of concrete weakly integral fusion categories and their canonical QCA-refined fusion rules
Equation

2.24
.
To date, there is no classification of weakly integral fusion categories. The main infinite series of examples are the Tambara-Yamagami categories and Metaplectic categories. A complete classification of modular weakly integral categories
4
4

4

A modular category is a non-degenerate unitary braided fusion category.
for rank
\leq 7
is obtained in
[
63
]
, which states any weakly integral modular category with
\text{rank}\leq 7
is a tensor product of pointed categories, Ising categories and Metaplectic
categories.
We now discuss the canonical QCA-refined realization for the Tambara-Yamagami (TY) categories, which are direct generalization of the Ising category, and the Metaplectic categories
SO(M)_{2}
.

Example 2.3
.

Tambara-Yamagami Fusion Categories.

Let
A
be an abelian group with
|A|
not a perfect square, and
\mathrm{TY}(A)
be a Tambara-Yamagami category. There are additional data such as the bicharacter and Frobenius-Schur indicator, which will not play a role here since they do not affect the fusion rules.
Denote the non-invertible simple by
m
, which has
\dim(m)=\sqrt{|A|}
and the invertible simples of dimension 1 by
a\in A
. The standard TY fusion rules are

m\otimes m=\bigoplus_{a\in A}a\,,\hskip 20.00003ptm\otimes a=a\otimes m=m

(2.25)

and the
a
fuse according to the group law in
A
.
Then its canonical QCA-refined fusion rules are

\displaystyle\mathsf{D}_{m}\mathsf{D}_{m}

\displaystyle=U_{|A|}\sum_{a\in A}\mathsf{D}_{a}

(2.26)

\displaystyle\mathsf{D}_{a}\mathsf{D}_{m}

\displaystyle=\mathsf{D}_{m}\mathsf{D}_{a}=\mathsf{D}_{m}\,,\hskip 20.00003pt\mathsf{D}_{a}\mathsf{D}_{b}=\mathsf{D}_{ab}\,.

We will construct the tensor-product Hilbert space realization of this in
Section

5
.

Example 2.4
.

Metaplectic Fusion Categories.

Another class of weakly integral fusion categories are the Metaplectic fusion categories
SO(M)_{2}
, whose complete categorical data have been calculated
[
64
,
65
]
.
They can be viewed as
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
-graded extensions of the representation category of the dihedral group
D_{M}
,
\mathbf{Rep}(D_{M})
, or alternatively as obtained from taking a
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
-equivariantization of the Drinfeld center
\mathcal{Z}(\mathbf{Rep}(D_{M}))
. We consider a Metaplectic fusion category
SO(M)_{2}
for odd
M=2r+1
. The simple objects are

\mathbf{1},\ Z,\ X,\ X^{\prime},\ Y_{1},\dots,Y_{r},\hskip 20.00003ptM=2r+1\,,

(2.27)

with quantum dimensions

\displaystyle\dim(\mathbf{1})

\displaystyle=\dim(Z)=1

(2.28)

\displaystyle\dim(X)

\displaystyle=\dim(X^{\prime})=\sqrt{M}

\displaystyle\dim(Y_{j})

\displaystyle=2\,.

Hence the total quantum dimension is

\displaystyle\dim(\mathcal{C})

\displaystyle=1^{2}+1^{2}+(\sqrt{M})^{2}+(\sqrt{M})^{2}+r\cdot 2^{2}

(2.29)

\displaystyle=2+2M+4\cdot\frac{M-1}{2}=4M\,.

So these categories are
weakly integral
. For

M
not a perfect square they are not integral. This can also be seen from the fact that
X
and
X^{\prime}
have non-integral quantum dimension

\sqrt{M}
whenever
M
is not a perfect square.
The fusion rules are:

\displaystyle Z\otimes Z

\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}

(2.30)

\displaystyle Y_{i}\otimes Y_{j}

\displaystyle=Y_{\min\{i+j,M-i-j\}}\oplus Y_{|i-j|}\hskip 20.00003pt(i\neq j),

\displaystyle Y_{i}\otimes Y_{i}

\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}\oplus Z\oplus Y_{\min\{2i,M-2i\}}

\displaystyle Z\otimes X

\displaystyle=X^{\prime},\hskip 20.00003ptZ\otimes X^{\prime}=X,\hskip 20.00003ptZ\otimes Y_{i}=Y_{i}

\displaystyle X\otimes X

\displaystyle=X^{\prime}\otimes X^{\prime}=\mathbf{1}\oplus\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r}Y_{i},\hskip 20.00003ptX\otimes X^{\prime}=Z\oplus\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r}Y_{i},

\displaystyle X\otimes Y_{i}

\displaystyle=X^{\prime}\otimes Y_{i}=X\oplus X^{\prime}\,.

The generators
1,Z,Y_{i},i=1,\cdots,r
form a fusion subcategory
\mathbf{Rep}(D_{M})

[
64
]
, as can be seen from the first three lines of the fusion rules above. The full
SO(M)_{2}
is a
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
-extension of this
\mathbf{Rep}(D_{M})
subcategory with the nontrivial component generated by
X,X^{\prime}
:

\mathcal{C}_{0}=\langle\mathbf{1},Z,Y_{1},\cdots,Y_{r}\rangle\,,\hskip 20.00003pt\mathcal{C}_{1}=\langle X,X^{\prime}\rangle\,.

(2.31)

We now consider the canonical QCA-refined fusion rules, assuming
M
is square-free. Following the convention in
Proposition

2.1
we have

n_{1}=M,\hskip 10.00002ptq(1,1)=M.

(2.32)

Then by
Equation

2.24
the canonical QCA-refined fusion rules are

\displaystyle\mathsf{D}_{X}\mathsf{D}_{X}

\displaystyle=\mathsf{D}_{X^{\prime}}\mathsf{D}_{X^{\prime}}=U_{M}\left(\mathsf{D}_{\mathbf{1}}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mathsf{D}_{Y_{i}}\right)

(2.33)

\displaystyle\mathsf{D}_{X}\mathsf{D}_{X^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=U_{M}\left(\mathsf{D}_{Z}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mathsf{D}_{Y_{i}}\right)\,,

where
U_{M}
is a QCA with index
M
, and the rest of the fusion rules stay the same as
Equation

2.30
. In particular, whenever both factors lie in the nontrivial graded component
\mathcal{C}_{1}
, the product acquires the QCA-refinement
U_{M}
, while all other products have trivial QCA-refinement. Finally the indices of symmetry operators in the canonical QCA-refined realization are

\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{\mathbf{1}})=\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{Y_{i}})=\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{Z})=1,\hskip 20.00003pt\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{X})=\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{X^{\prime}})=\sqrt{M}.

(2.34)

3
Lattice Model for Weakly Integral Fusion Categories

We now move on to present our
Result

2
. We will construct a lattice model that realizes any weakly integral fusion categories on a tensor-product Hilbert space up to QCAs, in the sense of
Definition

2.1
. Our construction is a generalization of the construction for integral fusion categories given in
[
42
]
, which we now review in a physicist-friendly way.

3.1
Lattice Model for Integral Fusion Categories

It is proven in
[
42
]
that a fusion categorical symmetry can be realized on a tensor-product Hilbert space strictly (without QCA refinement) if and only if it is integral. The “if" direction is proven by explicitly constructing a tensor-product realization of integral fusion categories. The construction is based on the anyon chain model, depicted in
Equation

3.1
.

,

,

,

is a unitary fusion category,

(3.1)

Our conventions for fusion diagrams are summarized in
Appendix

A
.
The vertical legs are labeled by the object
\rho\in\mathcal{C}
. The horizontal links have degrees of freedom labeled by simple objects
x_{i}\in\mathcal{M}
. For any fixed configuration of simple objects
\{x_{i}\}
, we assign a Hilbert space
V_{i}:=\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{M}}(x_{i}\lhd\rho,x_{i+1})
at each vertex. We choose the projection basis at each vertex:

|\nu_{i}\rangle=p_{x_{i+1}}^{\nu_{i}}:\hskip 10.00002ptx_{i}\otimes\rho\to x_{i+1},\hskip 10.00002pt\nu_{i}=1,\cdots,\dim(V_{i}).

(3.2)

The Hilbert space of an anyon chain with the above input is then

\mathcal{H}=\bigoplus_{\{x_{i}\in\mathcal{M}\}}\bigotimes_{i}\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{M}}(x_{i}\lhd\rho,x_{i+1}),

(3.3)

which is generally not a tensor product of local Hilbert spaces. Give an object
x\in\mathcal{C}
, the corresponding symmetry operator
\mathcal{D}_{x}
is defined by fusing with an
x
-line from above the anyon chain, and then deforming the diagram to a linear combination of the basis define before using
F
-moves:

(3.4)

Now let us assume
\mathcal{C}
is integral and take
\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{C}
to be the regular module category. The key observation is that in an integral fusion category the following object is well-defined,

R:=\bigoplus_{x\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C})}d_{x}x.

(3.5)

Here
d_{x}x
means
d_{x}
-fold direct sum of
x
:
d_{x}x=\oplus^{d_{x}}x
. This is well-defined because
d_{x}
is an integer. The object
R
is called the regular object in mathematics literature
[
61
]
. It has the crucial property that for any simple
z\in\mathcal{C}
,
z\otimes R=d_{z}R
. Indeed,

\displaystyle z\otimes R

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{x}d_{x}z\otimes x=\bigoplus_{x,y}d_{x}N^{y}_{zx}y

(3.6)

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{x,y}d_{x}N^{x}_{z^{*}y}y=\bigoplus_{y}d_{z}d_{y}y=d_{z}R.

This then implies

\dim\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(x\otimes R,y)=d_{x}d_{y},\hskip 10.00002pt\forall x,y\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}).

(3.7)

Then the Hilbert space
V_{i}
associated to a vertex can be decomposed into a tensor product
\mathbb{C}^{d_{x_{i}}}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{d_{x_{i+1}}}
. One pictures that the space
\mathbb{C}^{d_{x_{i}}}
now lives on the link
x_{i}
, and
\mathbb{C}^{d_{x_{i+1}}}
lives on the link
x_{i+1}
. The link
x_{i}
then hosts a Hilbert space
\mathbb{C}^{d_{x_{i}}^{2}}
. The total Hilbert space of the anyon chain is then

\mathcal{H}=\bigoplus_{\{x_{i}\in\mathcal{C}\}}\bigotimes_{i}\mathbb{C}^{d_{x_{i}}^{2}}=\bigotimes_{i}\mathbb{C}^{\sum_{x\in\mathcal{C}}d_{x}^{2}}=\bigotimes_{i}\mathbb{C}^{\dim(\mathcal{C})}\,,

(3.8)

which takes a tensor product form with on-site Hilbert space
\mathbb{C}^{\dim(\mathcal{C})}
. Diagrammatically, we have rearranged the vertex Hilbert spaces as follows:

(3.9)

This shows the anyon chain for an integral fusion category
\mathcal{C}
with input
(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{C},R)
has a tensor-product Hilbert space structure.

3.2
Lattice Model for Weakly Integral Fusion Categories

We now turn to a general weakly integral fusion category. Our construction is a combination of an anyon chain model similar to the previous one for integral fusion categories and an "anyonic" sequential circuit action. After discussing the Hilbert space structure of the modified anyon chain model, we will revisit the Ising category case to motivate our general construction that involves a sequential circuit action.

3.2.1
Setup

We now consider a weakly integral fusion category
\mathcal{C}=\oplus_{g\in E}\mathcal{C}_{g}
with its standard grading by
E
. Consider the anyon chain model as in
Equation

3.1
, but change
\rho
to

\rho=R_{0}:=\bigoplus_{x\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{0})}d_{x}x,

(3.10)

i.e., the regular object in the integral subcategory
\mathcal{C}_{0}
. Take
x\in\mathcal{C}_{g}
, we now have

\displaystyle x\otimes R_{0}

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{z\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{0})}d_{z}x\otimes z=\bigoplus_{z\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{0}),y\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{g})}d_{z}N^{y}_{xz}y

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{z\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{0}),y\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{g})}d_{z}N^{z}_{x^{*}y}y=\bigoplus_{y\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{g})}d_{x}d_{y}y.

(3.11)

Notice
d_{x}
and
d_{y}
may not be integers but
d_{x}d_{y}
is always an integer: write

d_{x}=a_{x}\sqrt{n_{g}}\,,\hskip 20.00003ptd_{y}=a_{y}\sqrt{n_{g}},

(3.12)

then we have

x\otimes R_{0}=n_{g}\bigoplus_{y\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{g})}a_{x}a_{y}y\,,

(3.13)

which implies for
x\in\mathcal{C}_{g},y\in\mathcal{C}_{h}

\dim\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(x\otimes R_{0},y)=\delta_{g,h}a_{x}a_{y}n_{g}.

(3.14)

This has the following consequences. First the total Hilbert space of the anyon chain now decomposes into
|E|
-many sectors:

\mathcal{H}=\bigoplus_{g\in E}\mathcal{H}_{g}.

(3.15)

This is because for
x_{i},x_{i+1}
belonging to different graded components of
\mathcal{C}
, we have
V_{i}=\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(x_{i}\otimes R_{0},x_{i+1})=0
. For each sector
g\in E
, the links have anyon labels
x_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{g}
. For fixed anyon configuration
\{x_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{g}\}
in the
g
-sector, the Hilbert space associated with a vertex has dimension

\dim\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(x_{i}\otimes R_{0},x_{i+1})=a_{x_{i}}a_{x_{i+1}}n_{g}.

(3.16)

We may now rearrange the vertex Hilbert spaces as in
Figure

1
.

(3.17)

Figure 1:
Rearranging the local Hilbert spaces for the anyon chain with a weakly-integral fusion category input. The red rectangle is a single site.

After this rearranging, each link
i
hosts a Hilbert space of dimension
a_{x_{i}}^{2}
. Let us define a site to be a vertex together with the adjacent link to its left. Then each site has dimension
a_{x_{i}}^{2}n_{g}
. Summing over the anyon configurations
\{x_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{g}\}
, the
g
-sector Hilbert space is

\mathcal{H}_{g}=\bigoplus_{\{x_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{g}\}}\bigotimes_{i}\mathbb{C}^{a_{x_{i}}^{2}n_{g}}=\bigotimes_{i}\mathbb{C}^{\sum_{x\in\mathcal{C}_{g}}a_{x}^{2}n_{g}}=\bigotimes_{i}\mathbb{C}^{\dim(\mathcal{C}_{g})}=\bigotimes_{i}\mathbb{C}^{\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})}.

(3.18)

We see that each sector
\mathcal{H}_{g}
is has a tensor product structure with on-site dimension
\dim(\mathcal{C}_{g})=\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})
. This means we have site-to-site isomorphism
\mathcal{H}_{g}\simeq\mathcal{H}_{0}
, which roughly speaking shifts a
\mathbb{C}^{n_{g}}
by half a site. Given a simple object
x\in\mathcal{C}_{g}
, we define the operator
\mathcal{D}_{x}
to be the usual action on
\mathcal{H}
by fusing with a line of
x
from above the anyon chain (
Equation

3.4
). It acts on sectors as

\mathcal{D}_{x}:\mathcal{H}_{h}\to\mathcal{H}_{gh}.

(3.19)

Since
\mathcal{H}=\oplus_{g\in E}\mathcal{H}_{g}
does not have a tensor product structure, the operators
\mathcal{D}_{x}
do not yet form a representation of
\mathcal{C}
on a single tensor-product Hilbert space.
Our strategy is to introduce locality-preserving isomorphisms
U_{g}:\mathcal{H}_{g}\simeq\mathcal{H}_{0}
in a coherent way so that the modified symmetry operators
\mathsf{D}_{x}:=U_{g}\circ\mathcal{D}_{x}|_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}:\mathcal{H}_{0}\to\mathcal{H}_{0}
form a representation of
\mathcal{C}
on a single tensor product space
\mathcal{H}_{0}
. It turns out this can be achieved at the cost of introducing QCA-refinement in the fusion rules.

Next we consider a simple example that illustrates the main idea, namely the Ising fusion category.

3.2.2
Ising Category Revisited

It is known that the Ising fusion category symmetry can be realized on a tensor-product Hilbert space, up to lattice translation; explicit lattice models can be found in
[
46
,
45
]
. Our goal here is to revisit this example in a way that makes the correct generalization to an arbitrary weakly integral fusion category transparent.

The Ising fusion category is weakly integral with grading
\mathrm{Ising}=\mathbf{Vec}_{\mathbb{Z}_{2}}\oplus\mathbf{Vec}
, and is a special case of the TY categories in
Example

2.3
with
A=\mathbb{Z}_{2}
.
Denote the invertible simples as
1,f
and the non-invertible simple as
\sigma
with
\sigma^{2}=1\oplus f
. We have
a_{1}=a_{f}=a_{\sigma}=1
and
n_{1}=n_{f}=1,n_{\sigma}=2
. The regular object of the integral subcategory is
R_{0}=1\oplus f
. Then the anyon chain with input
(\mathrm{Ising},\mathrm{Ising},1\oplus f)
has the Hilbert space structure

\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{H}_{1,f}\oplus\mathcal{H}_{\sigma}.

(3.20)

For the trivial sector
\mathcal{H}_{1,f}
, the links are labeled by
x_{i}\in\{1,f\}
. The vertex Hilbert space
V_{i}=\mathbb{C}
is one dimensional. Therefore the local Hilbert spaces can be associated with links and are
\mathbb{C}^{2}=\mathrm{Span}(|1\rangle,|f\rangle)
. See
Figure

2
.

(3.21)

Figure 2:
The trivial sector
\mathcal{H}_{1,f}
. At each link
x_{i}\in\{1,f\}
.

For the nontrivial sector
\mathcal{H}_{\sigma}
, the links have fixed anyon label
\sigma
. The vertex Hilbert space is
V_{i}=\mathbb{C}^{2}
, with a basis given by the two projections:

\text{id}_{\sigma}\otimes p_{1},~\text{id}_{\sigma}\otimes p_{f}:\hskip 10.00002pt\sigma\otimes(1\oplus f)\to\sigma.

(3.22)

We can place the projections on the vertical legs as shown in
Figure

3
. Then the on-site Hilbert space basis may be labeled as
|t_{i}\rangle\in\{1,f\}
:

(3.23)

Figure 3:
The nontrivial sector
\mathcal{H}_{\sigma}
. The basis for each on-site Hilbert space is
t_{i}\in\{1,f\}
. The black dots are unique projections.

The tensor product space
\mathcal{H}_{1,f}
forms a representation of the integral fusion subcategory
\mathcal{C}_{0}=\mathbf{Vec}_{\mathbb{Z}_{2}}
:

\mathcal{D}_{f}|\{x_{i}\}\rangle=|\{fx_{i}\}\rangle.

(3.24)

On the other hand the operator
\mathcal{D}_{\sigma}
maps
\mathcal{H}_{1,f}\to\mathcal{H}_{\sigma}
. We now calculate the operator
\mathcal{D}_{\sigma}
explicitly in the basis
|\{x_{i}\}\rangle
for
\mathcal{H}_{1,f}
and
|\{t_{i}\}\rangle
for
\mathcal{H}_{\sigma}
:

(3.34)

We conclude

U_{\sigma}|\{t_{i}\}\rangle_{\sigma}=\sum_{\{x_{i}\}}\prod_{i}H_{t_{i}x_{i}}|\{x_{i}\}\rangle_{1,f}\,.

(3.35)

We then define a modified symmetry operator
\mathsf{D}_{\sigma}:=U_{\sigma}\circ\mathcal{D}_{\sigma}:\mathcal{H}_{1,f}\to\mathcal{H}_{1,f}
,

\mathsf{D}_{\sigma}|\cdots,x_{i},x_{i+1},x_{i+2},\cdots\rangle_{1,f}=\prod_{k}H_{k}|\cdots,x_{i}x_{i+1},x_{i+1}x_{i+2},x_{i+2}x_{i+3},\cdots\rangle_{1,f}.

(3.36)

with the Hadamard gates
H_{k}
acting on site
k
. Notice that this precisely agrees with the Kramers-Wannier
duality operator defined in various papers in the literature
[
66
,
67
,
36
]
.

Our derivation of this operator provides a new perspective: The Kramers-Wannier
duality operator can be divided into the product of two operators, one is
\mathcal{D}_{\sigma}
which is defined by the fusing with anyon string as in the standard anyon chain model. The other operator is the product of the Hadamard gates, which comes from the action of a sequential circuit from below the anyon chain and is designed to map the image of
\mathcal{D}_{\sigma}
back to the tensor-product Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}_{1,f}
. Since actions from above the anyon chain commute with actions from below the anyon chain, we have

\mathsf{D}_{\sigma}\mathsf{D}_{\sigma}=U_{\sigma}^{2}\times\mathcal{D}_{\sigma}\mathcal{D}_{\sigma}=U_{\sigma}^{2}(\mathcal{D}_{1}+\mathcal{D}_{f}).

(3.37)

Given the expression
Equation

3.36
, it is known that
U_{\sigma}^{2}=T
is translation by one lattice site to the left. Here we provide a diagrammatic calculation. Observe that the sequential circuit
U_{\sigma}
may be redrawn as follows:

The circuit

We conclude that the Ising fusion category can indeed be realized on a tensor-product Hilbert space with on-site dimension 2, up to lattice translation. The mixing with lattice translation now acquires a new interpretation: it comes from a sequential circuit that acts on the anyon chain from below.

General Strategy.

This example suggests the following strategy for realizing a general weakly integral fusion categorical symmetry on a tensor-product Hilbert space:

•

Use the regular object
R_{0}
to build an anyon chain with Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}=\oplus_{g\in E}\mathcal{H}_{g}
, with each
\mathcal{H}_{g}
being a tensor-product Hilbert space.

•

For each
g\in E
, construct a sequential circuit
U_{g}
acting on the anyon chain from below such that it defines an isomorphism
\mathcal{H}_{g}\simeq\mathcal{H}_{0}
.

•

Then for each simple object
x\in\mathcal{C}_{g}
, define a modified symmetry operator
\mathsf{D}_{x}:=U_{g}\circ\mathcal{D}_{x}:\mathcal{H}_{0}\to\mathcal{H}_{0}
. Then we have modified fusion rules for
x\in\mathcal{C}_{g},~y\in\mathcal{C}_{h}
:

\mathsf{D}_{x}\circ\mathsf{D}_{y}=U_{g}\circ U_{h}\circ U_{gh}^{-1}\sum_{z\in\mathcal{C}_{gh}}N^{z}_{x,y}\mathsf{D}_{z}=U_{(g,h)}\sum_{z\in\mathcal{C}_{gh}}N^{z}_{x,y}\mathsf{D}_{z}

(3.39)

where
U_{(g,h)}:=U_{g}\circ U_{h}\circ U_{gh}^{-1}:\mathcal{H}_{0}\to\mathcal{H}_{0}
is now a QCA on
\mathcal{H}_{0}
. By construction, the QCA refinements
U_{(g,h)}
only depend on the sector labels
g,h
, and not specific anyons in the sectors. According to our
Theorem

2.1
, we expect

\mathrm{ind}(U_{(g,h)})=\sqrt{\frac{n_{g}n_{h}}{n_{gh}}}\frac{m_{g}m_{h}}{m_{gh}},

(3.40)

for some rational numbers
m_{g}
that also only depend on the sectors.

We now return to the construction for a general weakly integral fusion category following this strategy. We will then compute the indices of the QCAs
U_{(g,h)}
in
Section

4
and confirm that the above expectation is indeed true.

3.2.3
General Weakly Integral Categories

To complete the construction, it suffices to construct the sector-change sequential circuits
U_{g}:\mathcal{H}_{g}\to\mathcal{H}_{0}
. Below we will provide two constructions. The first one applies to a subclass of weakly integral fusion categories and has on-site Hilbert space dimension
\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})
. The second one applies to arbitrary weakly integral fusion categories but has a larger on-site dimension of
\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})^{2}
.

We begin by defining certain objects in a general weakly integral fusion category. Let
\mathcal{C}=\oplus_{g\in E}\mathcal{C}_{g}
be a weakly integral fusion category, and for every simple
x
we have
d_{x}=a_{x}\sqrt{n_{g}}
as before. Define for every
g\in E
an object

R_{g}:=\bigoplus_{x\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{g})}a_{x}x

(3.41)

which is the
g
-sector analog of the regular object
R_{0}
. It
has quantum dimension
d_{R_{g}}=\sqrt{n_{g}}\sum_{x\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{g})}a_{x}^{2}
. For
x\in\mathcal{C}_{g}
we have

\displaystyle x\otimes R_{h}

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{y\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{h})}a_{y}x\otimes y=\bigoplus_{y\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{h}),z\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{gh})}a_{y}N^{z}_{xy}z=\bigoplus_{y\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{h}),z\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{gh})}a_{y}N^{y}_{x^{*}z}z

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{z\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{gh})}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_{h}}}d_{x}d_{z}z=\sqrt{\frac{n_{g}n_{gh}}{n_{h}}}a_{x}R_{gh}\,.

(3.42)

One can also check that
R_{h}\otimes x=x\otimes R_{h}
. In particular we have

\displaystyle x\otimes R_{g}=R_{g}\otimes x=a_{x}R_{0},\hskip 20.00003ptx\otimes R_{0}=R_{0}\otimes x=n_{g}a_{x}R_{g},

(3.43)

\displaystyle R_{g}\otimes R_{g}=\bigoplus_{x\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{g})}a_{x}x\otimes R_{g}=\bigoplus_{x\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{g})}a_{x}^{2}R_{0}=\frac{\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})}{n_{g}}R_{0}\,.

(3.44)

Construction 1
.

Take
\rho=R_{0}
and build an anyon chain as before. Assume that for each
g\in E
, there exists an object
x_{g}\in\mathcal{C}_{g}
with
d_{x_{g}}=\sqrt{n_{g}}
(i.e.,
a_{x_{g}}=1
). Then we define a sequential circuit
U_{g}
as follows.

A unitary sequential circuit
U_{g}
that maps
\mathcal{H}_{g}\to\mathcal{H}_{0}
.

Notice that since
a_{x_{g}}=1
, we have
R_{g}\otimes x_{g}\simeq R_{0}\simeq x_{g}\otimes R_{g}
by
Equation

. We then take the red/blue dots to be unitary isomorphisms. Then clearly
U_{g}
is a unitary. Since the diagonal lines are
x_{g}\in\mathcal{C}_{g}
, this circuit maps
\mathcal{H}_{g}\to\mathcal{H}_{0}
. The condition of this construction is satisfied by Metaplectic categories
SO(M)_{2}
for odd square-free
M
and Tambara-Yamagami categories
\mathrm{TY}(A)
for
|A|
square free.

Remark 3.1
.

For a general weakly integral fusion category, we can replace
R_{0}
by
NR_{0}
where
N
is the minimal positive integer such that for any
g\in E
, there exists
x_{g}\in\mathcal{C}_{g}
with
a_{x_{g}}|N
. Then we can replace the vertical
R_{g}
by
(N/a_{x_{g}})R_{g}
. This works because we have isomorphisms
(N/a_{x_{g}})R_{g}\otimes x_{g}\simeq NR_{0}\simeq x_{g}\otimes(N/a_{x_{g}})R_{g}
. Alternatively, we have the following more uniform construction.

Construction 2
.

Now we do not make any assumption about the weakly integral fusion category. We take
\rho=\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})R_{0}
. This will lead to an anyon chain with Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}=\oplus_{g\in E}\mathcal{H}_{g}
and
\mathcal{H}_{g}
is a tensor product space with on-site dimension
\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})^{2}
. We then define the sequential circuit as in
Figure

7
.

that maps

.

(3.45)

Then clearly

.
We can take

Remark 3.2
.

Notice that the sequential circuits in both constructions take the form of "anyon translation". Namely, in
1
, the anyon
x_{g}
is translated to the left by one site (recall our circuit acts from below the anyon chain); in
2
, the anyon
R_{g}
is translated to the left by one site. This intuitive picture can be turned into a precise notion called generalized translation in
[
57
]
. We will discuss in more details the relation between our sequential circuits and generalized translation of
[
57
]
in
Section

4.3
.

Remark 3.3
.

The above two constructions are not the only possibilities. For specific examples one can be more flexible and construct other sequential circuits that do the job. The only requirement is that the anyon chain input is
\rho=NR_{0}
, i.e., some multiple of
R_{0}
and there exist pairs
X_{g},Y_{g}\in\mathcal{C}_{g}
for every
g\in E
such that
NR_{0}\simeq X_{g}\otimes Y_{g}\simeq Y_{g}\otimes X_{g}
, then one can take the sequential circuit
U_{g}
to be “translating
Y_{g}
by one site".

Remark 3.4
.

In fact the modified operators
\mathsf{D}_{x}=U_{g}\circ\mathcal{D}_{x},~x\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{g})
fix each component
\mathcal{H}_{h}
in the direct sum
\mathcal{H}=\oplus_{h\in E}\mathcal{H}_{h}
. Hence more generally one could consider the restriction of the operators
\{\mathsf{D}_{x}:x\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C})\}
to the subspace
\mathcal{H}_{h}
, which would give a QCA-refined realization on the tensor-product Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}_{h}
.

3.2.4
Some Technical Aspects of the Constructions

Here we discuss some technical details of the general constructions above that are not visible in the simple Ising category example. We highlight some subtleties one needs to pay attention to if one wishes to concretely implement the constructions for more complicated weakly integral categories such as the Metaplectic categories. We will follow
1
for illustration.

Choice of isomorphisms
\delta,\gamma
.

In the definition of the sequential circuit
U_{g}
, a pair of isomorphisms

\gamma_{g}:R_{0}\to R_{g}\otimes x_{g},\hskip 10.00002pt\delta_{g}:x_{g}\otimes R_{g}\to R_{0}.

(3.46)

must be chosen. Here we explain the meaning of making such a choice. We can expand these isomorphisms in a basis consisting of compositions of inclusion/projection of simples as below:

(3.47)

Here
t\in R_{g}
label simple summads of
R_{g}
,
s\in R_{0}
label simple summads of
R_{0}
, and
i_{t}^{\nu},p_{s}^{\mu},i_{s}^{\nu},p_{t}^{\mu}
are inclusions/projections. We have assumed the fusion category is multiplicity-free. The summations run over configurations such that the trivalent vertex Hilbert space is nonzero, i.e.,
\text{Hom}(s,t\otimes x_{g})\neq 0
for the left diagram and
\text{Hom}(x_{g}\otimes t,s)\neq 0
for the right diagram.
The coefficients
(\gamma_{g})^{st}_{\mu\nu},(\delta_{g})_{\mu\nu}^{st}
are the choices here. They must be chosen so that
\gamma_{g},\delta_{g}
are unitaries. In general there is no natural choice for them, one simply needs to make one. Once the coefficients have been chosen, one can then calculate the action of the sequential circuit using standard diagrammatics of unitary fusion category that only involve simple objects.

Choice of on-site basis

To express the symmetry operator
\mathsf{D}_{x}=U_{g}\circ\mathcal{D}_{x}
explicitly as an operator acting on the tensor-product Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}_{0}
requires choosing a basis for the on-site Hilbert space. The basis of the anyon chain Hilbert space that is natural for diagrammatic computation does not show the tensor product structure explicitly, hence one needs to perform a basis change. The anyon chain
(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{C},R_{0})
has a Hilbert space structure
\mathcal{H}=\oplus_{g}\mathcal{H}_{g}
. To illustrate the idea, let us consider the case
\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{H}_{0}\oplus\mathcal{H}_{1}
is
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
-graded. The subspace
\mathcal{H}_{0}
has a basis represented as below where the red rectangle indicates the basis for a single site.

(3.48)

From
Equation

3.14
we know the Hilbert space at the vertex between
s_{k}
and
s_{k+1}
has dimension
d_{s_{k}}d_{s_{k+1}}
. Hence we can choose a basis with the following index structure:

|\mu_{k}^{s_{k}},\mu_{k}^{s_{k+1}}\rangle:\mu_{k}^{s_{k}}=1,\cdots,d_{s_{k}};\mu_{k}^{s_{k+1}}=1,\cdots,d_{s_{k+1}}.

(3.49)

The basis for a single site is then

|\mu_{k}^{s_{k+1}},s_{k+1},\mu_{k+1}^{s_{k+1}}\rangle:s_{k+1}\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{0});\mu_{k}^{s_{k+1}}=1,\cdots,d_{s_{k+1}};\mu_{k}^{s_{k+1}}=1,\cdots,d_{s_{k+1}},

(3.50)

as indicated by the red rectangle in
Equation

3.48
. This is a basis that makes the tensor product structure of
\mathcal{H}_{0}
transparent. However the natural basis for performing diagrammatic calculation is the following:

(3.51)

Here
\xi_{k}\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{0})
are simple objects such that
s_{k+1}\in s_{k}\otimes\xi_{k}
and

\epsilon_{k}=1,\cdots,d_{\xi_{k}}:R_{0}\to\xi_{k}

(3.52)

label orthonormal projections. We again assumed multiplicity-free. We then have a natural basis
\{|\xi_{k},\epsilon_{k}\rangle\}
for
\text{Hom}(s_{k}\otimes R_{0},s_{k+1})
. There should be
d_{s_{k}}d_{s_{k+1}}
many admissible values of
(\xi_{k},\epsilon_{k})
. We then need to specify how the previous basis
\{|\mu_{k}^{s_{k}},\mu_{k}^{s_{k+1}}\rangle\}
is related to this basis. For instance, we can simply choose the previous basis
\{|\mu_{k}^{s_{k}},\mu_{k}^{s_{k+1}}\rangle\}
to be related to this projection basis by relabeling. That is, we take some bijection of sets

\gamma_{s_{k},s_{k+1}}:[d_{s_{k}}]\times[d_{s_{k+1}}]\to\{(\xi_{k},\epsilon_{k}):s_{k+1}\in s_{k}\otimes\xi_{k},\epsilon_{k}=1,\cdots,d_{\xi_{k}}\}

(3.53)

and identify

|\gamma_{s_{k},s_{k+1}}(\mu_{k}^{s_{k}},\mu_{k}^{s_{k+1}})\rangle=|\mu_{k}^{s_{k}},\mu_{k}^{s_{k+1}}\rangle.

and

has dimension

with the following index structure :

|\nu_{k}^{t_{k}},\sigma_{k},\nu_{k}^{t_{k+1}}\rangle:\nu_{k}^{t}=1,\cdots,a_{t};\sigma_{k}=1,\cdots,n_{1}.

(3.56)

(3.57)

Here
\xi_{k}\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{0})
takes values in anyons such that
t_{k+1}\in t_{k}\otimes\xi_{k}
, and
\eta_{k}\in 1,\cdots,d_{\xi_{k}}
label orthonormal projections. This gives us a natural basis
|\xi_{k},\eta_{k}\rangle
for
\text{Hom}(t_{k}\otimes R_{0},t_{k+1})
. We can then choose some bijection of sets

\gamma_{t_{k},t_{k+1}}:[a_{t}]\times[n_{1}]\times[a_{t+1}]\to\{(\xi_{k},\eta_{k}):t_{k+1}\in t_{k}\otimes\xi_{k},\eta_{k}\in 1,\cdots,d_{\xi_{k}}\}

(3.58)

and identify

|\gamma_{t_{k},t_{k+1}}(\nu_{k}^{t_{k}},\sigma_{k},\nu_{k}^{t_{k+1}})\rangle=|\nu_{k}^{t_{k}},\sigma_{k},\nu_{k}^{t_{k+1}}\rangle.

(3.59)

In other words the two basis are related by relabeling. In practice, one should perform calculation of
\mathsf{D}_{x}
first in the basis given by projections onto simples (
Equation

3.51
and
Equation

3.57
) via standard diagrammatics, then do a basis change to the tensor-product basis to reveal the tensor-product structure of the symmetry operator.

4
Indices of Symmetry Operators

We now compute the indices of the symmetry operators in the lattice models obtained by
2
.
We will show that the index of
\mathsf{D}_{x}
for
x\in\mathcal{C}_{g}
is given by

\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{x})=\dim(R_{g})^{-1}=m_{x}\sqrt{n_{g}},\hskip 10.00002ptm_{x}\coloneq\frac{1}{\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})}\,.

(4.1)

We note that the index of
\mathsf{D}_{x}
agrees with the dimension of the object translated by the sequential circuit in
Figure

7
.
5
5

5

Similarly, one can also show that the index of
\mathsf{D}_{x}
in
1
is given by
\dim(x_{g})^{-1}=\sqrt{n_{g}}^{-1}
, where
x_{g}
is the object translated to the left in
Figure

6
. In this section, we will focus only on
2
.

Furthermore, we will also show that the index of QCA
U_{(g,h)}
appearing in the lattice-level fusion rules
Equation

3.39
is given by

\mathrm{ind}(U_{(g,h)})=\frac{\dim(R_{gh})}{\dim(R_{g})\dim(R_{h})}=\frac{m_{x}m_{y}}{m_{z}}\sqrt{\frac{n_{g}n_{h}}{n_{gh}}}.

(4.2)

This result agrees with the prediction of
Theorem

2.1
.

In what follows, the symmetry operators on the graded Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}=\bigoplus_{h\in E}\mathcal{H}_{h}
are denoted by
\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x}\coloneq U_{g}\mathcal{D}_{x}
, while the symmetry operators on a single sector
\mathcal{H}_{0}
are denoted by
\mathsf{D}_{x}\coloneq\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x}|_{\mathcal{H}_{0}}
.
Here,
\mathcal{D}_{x}:\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{H}
is the standard symmetry operator defined by
Equation

3.4
.
We note that
\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x}
preserves the grading, while
\mathcal{D}_{x}
does not.

4.1
Defect Hilbert spaces

To compute the index of
\mathsf{D}_{x}
, we first define the left and right defect Hilbert spaces for
\mathsf{D}_{x}
.
To this end, we first recall the definition of the defect Hilbert spaces in the anyon chains
[

(4.3)

Here, the horizontal edges are labeled by objects of
\mathcal{C}
.
The right defect Hilbert space is defined in the same way by flipping the orientation of the defect labeled by
x
.
We denote the number of vertical legs below the chain by
L
.

The defect Hilbert space for the symmetry operator
\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x}=U_{g}\mathcal{D}_{x}
is obtained by further inserting a
U_{g}
-defect that ends on the chain from below.
The insertion of a
U_{g}
-defect is done by following the definition of the defect Hilbert space for a sequential circuit
[
51
]
.
More specifically, we define the left defect Hilbert space for
\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x}
by the vector space of morphisms represented by the following fusion diagrams:

4.6
, there is no factor of

We note that the product of the above local unitaries acts in the same way as
U_{g}^{\dagger}
, up to defect creation and annihilation operators.

4.4
and

(4.11)

Namely, the left defect Hilbert space for
\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x}
is obtained by inserting an
x
-defect from above, removing a single leg labeled by
\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})R_{0}
, and adding an
n_{g}R_{g}
-defect from below.
Since the removed leg is labeled by
\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})R_{0}\cong n_{g}R_{g}\otimes R_{g}
, removing a single leg and adding an
n_{g}R_{g}
-defect is equivalent to removing a single
R_{g}
-defect.
We note that the number of vertical legs for
\mathcal{H}_{\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x}}^{l}
is one less than that for
\mathcal{H}_{\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x}}^{r}
.

As in the case of no defect, all horizontal edges in the fusion diagrams (
4.11
) and (
4.10
) have the same grading.
Thus, the defect Hilbert spaces
\mathcal{H}_{\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x}}^{l}
and
\mathcal{H}_{\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x}}^{r}
are graded by
E
, i.e.,

\mathcal{H}_{\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x}}^{l}=\bigoplus_{h\in E}(\mathcal{H}_{\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x}}^{l})_{h},\hskip 20.00003pt\mathcal{H}_{\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x}}^{r}=\bigoplus_{h\in E}(\mathcal{H}_{\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x}}^{r})_{h},

(4.12)

where
h\in E
is the grading of the objects on the horizontal edges.
Based on this decomposition, we define the left and right defect Hilbert spaces for the symmetry operator
\mathsf{D}_{x}:\mathcal{H}_{0}\to\mathcal{H}_{0}
on the trivially graded sector by

\mathcal{H}_{\mathsf{D}_{x}}^{l}\coloneq(\mathcal{H}_{\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x}}^{l})_{0},\hskip 20.00003pt\mathcal{H}_{\mathsf{D}_{x}}^{r}\coloneq(\mathcal{H}_{\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x}}^{r})_{0}.

(4.13)

Tensor product decomposition.

The defect Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}_{\mathsf{D}_{x}}^{l}
defined above admits a tensor product decomposition.
More generally, for every
h\in E
, the
h
-graded component of
\mathcal{H}_{\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x}}^{l}
admits a tensor product decomposition.
To see this, we recall that each state in the
h
-graded component of
\mathcal{H}_{\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x}}^{l}
is represented by a fusion diagram in
Equation

4.11
whose horizontal edges are labeled by objects of
\mathcal{C}_{h}
.
For fixed labels of the horizontal edges, the Hilbert space associated with each vertex away from the defect has dimension

\dim\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(x_{i}\otimes\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})R_{0},x_{i+1})=\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})\dim(x_{i})\dim(x_{i+1})=\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})n_{h}a_{x_{i}}a_{x_{i+1}},

(4.14)

where
x_{i},x_{i+1}\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{h})
are the labels of the left and right edges connected to the vertex.
This Hilbert space can be factorized into the tensor product of three Hilbert spaces assigned to the vertex and the two adjacent edges as follows:

(4.15)

On the other hand, the Hilbert space associated with the vertex at the defect locus has dimension

\dim\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(x_{i}\otimes n_{g}R_{g},x\otimes x_{i}^{\prime})=\dim(x)\dim(x_{i})\dim(x_{i}^{\prime})\sqrt{n_{g}}=n_{g}a_{x}n_{h}a_{x_{i}}a_{x_{i}^{\prime}},

(4.16)

where
x_{i},x_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{h})
are the labels of the left and right edges connected to the vertex.
This Hilbert space can also be factorized into the tensor product of three Hilbert spaces as

(4.17)

Equation

4.15
and
Equation

4.17
imply the following decomposition of the Hilbert space for fixed labels: each edge has a Hilbert space of dimension
n_{h}a_{x_{i}}^{2}=\dim(x_{i})^{2}
, each vertex except for the one on the defect has a Hilbert space of dimension
\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})
, and the vertex at the defect locus has a Hilbert space of dimension
n_{g}a_{x}
.
By taking the direct sum over all labels in
\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{h})
, the dimension of the Hilbert space on each edge becomes
\sum_{x_{i}\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{h})}\dim(x_{i})^{2}=\dim(\mathcal{C}_{h})=\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})
.
Now, we define a site by the pair of a vertex and the adjacent edge on its left.
If a site contains a vertex at the defect locus, the on-site dimension is
n_{g}a_{x}\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})
.
Otherwise, the on-site dimension is
\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})^{2}
.
Thus, the
h
-graded component of
\mathcal{H}_{\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x}}^{l}
can be written as

(\mathcal{H}_{\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x}}^{l})_{h}\cong\mathbb{C}^{n_{g}a_{x}\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})}\otimes\bigotimes_{i=1}^{L-1}\mathbb{C}^{\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})^{2}}.

(4.18)

Here, we recall that the number of vertical legs in
Equation

4.11
is
L-1
.
A similar computation shows that the
h
-graded component of
\mathcal{H}_{\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x}}^{r}
is given by

(\mathcal{H}_{\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{x}}^{r})_{h}\cong\mathbb{C}^{a_{x}\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})}\otimes\bigotimes_{i=1}^{L}\mathbb{C}^{\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})^{2}}.

(4.19)

We note that the Hilbert spaces (
4.18
) and (
4.19
) do not depend on the grading
h\in E
up to isomorphism.
In particular, the trivially graded components are given by

\mathcal{H}_{\mathsf{D}_{x}}^{l}\cong\mathbb{C}^{n_{g}a_{x}\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})}\otimes\bigotimes_{i=1}^{L-1}\mathbb{C}^{\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})^{2}},\hskip 20.00003pt\mathcal{H}_{\mathsf{D}_{x}}^{r}\cong\mathbb{C}^{a_{x}\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})}\otimes\bigotimes_{i=1}^{L}\mathbb{C}^{\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})^{2}}.

(4.20)

4.2
Indices

Index of symmetry operator
\mathsf{D}_{x}
.

Based on the above definition of the defect Hilbert spaces, we can now compute the indices of the symmetry operators.
The tensor product decomposition in
Equation

4.20
implies that the left and right dimensions of
\mathsf{D}_{x}
for
x\in\mathcal{C}_{g}
are given by

\mathrm{ldim}(\mathsf{D}_{x})=\frac{n_{g}a_{x}}{\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})}=\frac{\dim(x)}{\dim(R_{g})},\hskip 20.00003pt\mathrm{rdim}(\mathsf{D}_{x})=a_{x}\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})=\dim(x)\dim(R_{g}).

(4.21)

Therefore, the index of
\mathsf{D}_{x}
can be computed as

\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{x})=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{ldim}(\mathsf{D}_{x})}{\mathrm{rdim}(\mathsf{D}_{x})}}=\dim(R_{g})^{-1}=\frac{\sqrt{n_{g}}}{\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})}.

(4.22)

In particular, the irrational part of
\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{x})
is
\sqrt{n_{g}}
, as predicted in
Theorem

2.1
.

The index of
\mathsf{D}_{x}
computed above depends only on the grading of
x\in\mathcal{C}_{g}
.
This implies that the index is homogeneous.
Indeed, for the lattice-level fusion rules (
3.39
), all fusion channels
U_{(g,h)}\mathsf{D}_{z}
with
z\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C}_{gh})
have the same index because the indices of both
U_{(g,h)}
and
\mathsf{D}_{z}
depend only on the grading.
Here, we recall
U_{(g,h)}\coloneq U_{g}U_{h}U_{gh}^{-1}
.
In what follows, we will explicitly compute
\mathrm{ind}(U_{(g,h)})
and show that the index satisfies

\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{x})\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{y})=\mathrm{ind}(U_{(g,h)})\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{z})

(4.23)

for all fusion channels.

Index of QCA
U_{(g,h)}
.

To compute the index of
U_{(g,h)}
, we first define the left and right defect Hilbert spaces for
U_{(g,h)}
.
Following the definition of the
U_{g}
-defect discussed above, we define the left defect Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}^{l}_{U_{(g,h)}}
by the vector space of morphisms represented by the following fusion diagrams:

(4.27)

where the number of the vertical legs except for the defects is
L-1
.

From the above definition of the defect Hilbert spaces, we can compute the left and right dimensions of
U_{(g,h)}
as

\displaystyle\mathrm{ldim}(U_{(g,h)})

\displaystyle=\frac{\dim(n_{g}R_{g})\dim(n_{h}R_{h})\dim(R_{gh})}{\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})^{2}\dim(R_{0})^{2}}=\frac{\dim(R_{gh})}{\dim(R_{g})\dim(R_{h})},

(4.28)

\displaystyle\mathrm{rdim}(U_{(g,h)})

\displaystyle=\frac{\dim(n_{gh}R_{gh})\dim(R_{g})\dim(R_{h})}{\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})\dim(R_{0})}=\frac{\dim(R_{g})\dim(R_{h})}{\dim(R_{gh})}.

(4.29)

Thus, the index of
U_{(g,h)}
is given by

\mathrm{ind}(U_{(g,h)})=\frac{\dim(R_{gh})}{\dim(R_{g})\dim(R_{h})}=\frac{m_{g}m_{h}}{m_{gh}}\sqrt{\frac{n_{g}n_{h}}{n_{gh}}},

(4.30)

where
m_{g}\coloneq\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})^{-1}
for all
g\in E
.
We note that this index agrees with our expectation in
Equation

3.40
.
Based on
Equation

4.22
and
Equation

4.30
, we can compute the product of indices as

\mathrm{ind}(U_{(g,h)})\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{z})=\sqrt{n_{g}n_{h}}m_{g}m_{h}=\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{x})\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{y}),

(4.31)

which shows
Equation

4.23
.

4.3
Relation to the QCA index of Jones and Lim

In
[
57
]
, Jones and Lim defined an index of QCAs on the anyon chain using operator algebras.
As we will see below, our index of non-invertible symmetry operator
\mathsf{D}_{x}
for
x\in\mathcal{C}_{g}
is related to the QCA index of Jones and Lim by

\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{x})=\mathrm{ind}_{\mathrm{JL}}(U_{g}),

(4.32)

where
\mathrm{ind}_{\mathrm{JL}}
denotes the index defined in
[
57
]
and
U_{g}
is the sequential circuit in
Figure

7
.
Furthermore, since
\mathrm{ind}_{\mathrm{JL}}
is multiplicative
[
57
]
, the composite operator
U_{(g,h)}=U_{g}U_{h}U_{gh}^{-1}
has the index

\mathrm{ind}_{\mathrm{JL}}(U_{(g,h)})=\frac{\dim(R_{gh})}{\dim(R_{g})\dim(R_{h})}=\mathrm{ind}(U_{(g,h)}),

(4.33)

which shows that
\mathrm{ind}_{\mathrm{JL}}
agrees with our index when evaluated on a QCA
U_{(g,h)}
.

In the remaining of this subsection, we show
Equation

4.32
.
To this end, we first show that
U_{g}
is an example of a generalized translation defined in
[
57
]
.
We can then apply the index formula in
[
57
, Proposition 4.1]
to compute the index of
U_{g}
.

Generalized translation.

Let us first recall the definition of generalized translations.
We consider an anyon chain based on a fusion category
\mathcal{C}
and an input object
\rho\in\mathcal{C}_{0}
.
8
8

8

We do not specify the choice of a
\mathcal{C}
-module category because it is not relevant to the following discussions.

Here,
\mathcal{C}_{0}
is a fusion subcategory of
\mathcal{C}
.
For our purposes, it suffices to take
\mathcal{C}
to be a weakly integral fusion category and
\mathcal{C}_{0}
to be its integral subcategory.
We suppose that there exists a pair of objects
y,z\in\mathcal{C}
such that

\rho\cong y\otimes z\cong z\otimes y.

(4.34)

We also choose an isomorphism

\sigma:y\otimes z\to z\otimes y.

(4.35)

Using the above data, we can define a generalized translation
\alpha
as a QCA on the algebra of local operators.
To define
\alpha
, we consider its action on local operators supported on a finite interval
I=[i_{0},i_{1}]
of length
m
.
Here,
i_{0}
and
i_{1}
are the left and right ends of
I
.
The generalized translation
\alpha
maps local operators on
I
to those supported on
I^{+1}=[i_{0}-1,i_{1}+1]
.
The action of
\alpha
on a local operator
w\in\mathrm{End}(\rho^{\otimes m})
supported on
I
is defined by
[
57
]

\alpha(w)=\text{id}_{\rho}\otimes\text{id}_{y}\otimes(\sigma^{\otimes m}\circ w\circ(\sigma^{-1})^{\otimes m})\otimes\text{id}_{z}.

(4.36)

Here, as in the original paper
[
57
]
, we implicitly chose an isomorphism between
\rho
and
y\otimes z
.
If we make this choice explicit, the above expression becomes

\alpha(w)=(\text{id}_{\rho}\otimes(s^{-1})^{\otimes m+1})\circ(\text{id}_{\rho}\otimes\text{id}_{y}\otimes(\sigma^{\otimes m}\circ s(w)\circ(\sigma^{-1})^{\otimes m})\otimes\text{id}_{z})\circ(\text{id}_{\rho}\otimes s^{\otimes m+1}),

(4.37)

where
s:\rho\to y\otimes z
is an isomorphism and
s(w)\coloneq s^{\otimes m}\circ w\circ(s^{-1})^{\otimes m}
.
One can also write the above
\alpha(w)
as

\alpha(w)=(\text{id}_{\rho}\otimes(s^{-1})^{\otimes m+1})\circ(\text{id}_{\rho}\otimes\text{id}_{y}\otimes(t^{\otimes m}\circ w\circ(t^{-1})^{\otimes m})\otimes\text{id}_{z})\circ(\text{id}_{\rho}\otimes s^{\otimes m+1}),

(4.38)

where
t:\rho\to z\otimes y
is an isomorphism defined by
t\coloneq\sigma\circ s
.

To see the relation between generalized translation
\alpha
and our sequential circuit
U_{g}
, it is helpful to represent
\alpha(w)
diagrammatically as follows:

(4.41)

We note that
U^{-1}
acts first and
U
acts last in
Equation

4.40
because
\alpha(w)
in
Equation

4.39
acts on the chain from below.
The unitary
U
defined above is related to our sequential circuit
U_{g}
as

U=T_{+}U_{g},

(4.42)

where
T_{+}
is a lattice translation by one site to the right, and we identified

\rho=\dim(\mathcal{C}_{0})R_{0},\hskip 10.00002pty=n_{g}R_{g},\hskip 10.00002ptz=R_{g},\hskip 10.00002pts=\gamma_{g},\hskip 10.00002ptt=\delta_{g}^{\dagger}.

(4.43)

Equation (
4.42
) shows that the sequential circuit
U_{g}
is an example of a generalized translation.

Index of
U_{g}
.

Now, we can compute
\mathrm{ind}_{\mathrm{JL}}(U_{g})
by applying the index formula in
[
57
, Proposition 4.1]
.
Since
\mathrm{ind}_{\mathrm{JL}}
is multiplicative
[
57
]
,
Equation

4.42
implies

\mathrm{ind}_{\mathrm{JL}}(U_{g})=\frac{\mathrm{ind}_{\mathrm{JL}}(U)}{\mathrm{ind}_{\mathrm{JL}}(T_{+})}.

(4.44)

Furtehrmore, due to
[
57
, Proposition 4.1]
, the indices of
U
and
T_{+}
are given by

\mathrm{ind}_{\mathrm{JL}}(U)=\dim(n_{g}R_{g}),\hskip 20.00003pt\mathrm{ind}_{\mathrm{JL}}(T_{+})=\dim(\rho)=\dim(n_{g}R_{g})\dim(R_{g}).

(4.45)

By plugging these into
Equation

4.44
, we find

\mathrm{ind}_{\mathrm{JL}}(U_{g})=\dim(R_{g})^{-1}.

(4.46)

In particular, due to
Equation

4.22
, we have
\mathrm{ind}_{\mathrm{JL}}(U_{g})=\mathrm{ind}(\mathsf{D}_{x})
for all
x\in\mathcal{C}_{g}
, which shows
Equation

4.32
.

5
Tensor Product Realization of General Tambara-Yamagami Categories

We now apply our general construction in
Section

3.2
to the class of general Tambara-Yamagami fusion categories. We calculate the explicit expressions of symmetry operators and the QCA refinement following
1
. Tambara-Yamagami categories of the form
\mathrm{TY}(\mathbb{Z}_{N})
have been realized on a tensor-product Hilbert space
[
48
]
. Here we are not restricted to such cases and consider general Tambara-Yamagami categories. We start by reviewing the basic structures of general Tambara-Yamagami fusion categories.

5.1
Review of Tambara-Yamagami Categories

A Tambara–Yamagami category

[
62
]
is a
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
-graded fusion category
\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{C}_{0}\oplus\mathcal{C}_{1}
with
\mathcal{C}_{0}=\mathbf{Vec}_{A},~\mathcal{C}_{1}=\mathbf{Vec}
, where
A
is a finite abelian group. We denote the simple objects in
\mathbf{Vec}_{A}
as
a\in A
and the simple object in the nontrivial component as
m
. Then the fusion rules is

a\otimes b=ab,~a\otimes m=m\otimes a=m,~m\otimes m=\oplus_{a\in A}a.

(5.1)

A Tambara–Yamagami category of the above form is parameterized by (1). A symmetric non-degenerate bicharacter
\chi:A\times A\to U(1)
. (2). A Frobenius-Schur indicator
\epsilon=\pm
. We denote the corresponding fusion category as
\mathrm{TY}(A,\chi,\epsilon)
. The quantum dimensions of simples are

\dim(a)=1\hskip 10.00002pt\forall\,a\in A,\hskip 20.00003pt\dim(m)=\sqrt{|A|}.

(5.2)

The global quantum dimension of
\mathrm{TY}(A,\chi,\epsilon)
is thus

\dim\bigl(\mathrm{TY}(A,\chi,\epsilon)\bigr)=\sum_{a\in A}\dim(a)^{2}+\dim(m)^{2}=2|A|,

(5.3)

which shows the fusion category
\mathrm{TY}(A,\chi,\epsilon)
is weakly integral.

F
-Symbols.

The associativity constraints are largely trivial. The complete list of non-trivial
F
-symbols was obtained in
[
62
]
. The ones relevant for us are:

F^{mab}_{m}=1,\hskip 20.00003ptF^{amm}_{b}=1,

(5.4)

and

(F^{mmm}_{m})_{ab}=\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{|A|}}\chi(a,b).

(5.5)

Example 5.1
.

Take
A=\mathbb{Z}_{N}=\{0,1,\cdots,N-1\}
, then symmetric bicharacters are classified by
\mathbb{Z}_{N}
, for
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{N}
the corresponding bicharacter
\chi_{k}
takes the form

\chi_{k}(a,b)=\exp\left(\frac{2\pi ik}{N}ab\right).

(5.6)

This bicharacter is non-degenerate precisely when
\mathrm{gcd}(k,N)=1
. The
F
-symbol

(F^{mmm}_{m})_{ab}=\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{N}}\exp\left(\frac{2\pi ik}{N}ab\right)

(5.7)

is nothing but the normalized discrete Fourier transformation, up to the sign
\epsilon
.

5.2
Tensor-product Hilbert Space Realization

We now provide an explicit QCA-refined tensor-product realization of a general Tambara-Yamagami category. If
|A|
is a perfect square then
\mathrm{TY}(A,\chi,\epsilon)
is integral and admits a strict tensor-product realization. Hence we only consider the case where
|A|
is not a perfect square. Then the integral subcategory
\mathsf{Vec}_{A}
has total quantum dimension
|A|
, and we will realize the symmetry
\mathrm{TY}(A,\chi,\epsilon)
on a tensor-product Hilbert space with on-site dimension
|A|
.

For a generic abelian group
A
we can not apply our
1
:
a_{m}
is the integer part of
d_{m}=\sqrt{|A|}
, which is not 1 unless
|A|
is square-free. We will instead consider the “flexible construction" in
Remark

3.3
. The construction will be a natural generalization of the Ising category example in
Section

3.2.2
. For example, the sequential circuit
U_{1}
will be similar to
Figure

4
with
\sigma
replaced by
m
. We start with the anyon chain Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{H}_{0}\oplus\mathcal{H}_{1}
built from choosing

\rho=R_{0}=\bigoplus_{a\in A}a.

(5.8)

The subspace
\mathcal{H}_{0}
has a basis similar to
Figure

2
but with
x_{i}\in A
, and
\mathcal{H}_{1}
has a basis similar to
Figure

3
with
t_{i}\in A
. The basis vectors are denoted as

|\{x_{i}\}\rangle_{0}\in\mathcal{H}_{0},\hskip 10.00002pt|\{t_{i}\}\rangle_{1}\in\mathcal{H}_{1}.

(5.9)

The integral subcategory
\mathbf{Vec}_{A}
is represented on
\mathcal{H}_{0}
directly by anyon fusion action as in
Equation

3.4
. We have

\displaystyle\mathsf{D}_{a}|\{x_{i}\}\rangle_{0}=|\{ax_{i}\}\rangle_{0}.

(5.10)

The symmetry action for the noninvertible anyon
m
is
\mathsf{D}_{m}=U_{1}\circ\mathcal{D}_{m}
. The operator
\mathcal{D}_{m}:\mathcal{H}_{0}\to\mathcal{H}_{1}
may be calculated in a similar fashion as in
Equation

3.25
, where the relevant
F
-symbol is
F^{mab}_{m}=1
, and maps
\mathcal{H}_{0}\to\mathcal{H}_{1}
. We arrive at

\mathcal{D}_{m}|\cdots,x_{i},x_{i+1},x_{i+2},\cdots\rangle_{0}=|\cdots,x_{i}^{-1}x_{i+1},x_{i+1}^{-1}x_{i+2},x_{i+2}^{-1}x_{i+3},\cdots\rangle_{1}.

(5.11)

The sequential circuit
U_{1}
is defined similar to
Figure

4
with
\sigma
replaced by
m
. The action of the sequential circuit
U_{1}
can be calculated similar to that in
Equation

3.31
. The relevant
F
-symbols for this calculation are
F^{mmm}_{m}
(
Equation

5.5
) and
F^{amm}_{b}=1
. The action is thus

U_{1}|\{t_{i}\}\rangle_{1}=\left(\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{|A|}}\right)^{L}\sum_{\{x_{i}\}}\prod_{i}\chi(t_{i},x_{i})|\{x_{i}\}\rangle_{0}.

(5.12)

The combined action is therefore

\boxed{\mathsf{D}_{m}|\{x_{i}\}\rangle_{0}=U_{1}\circ\mathcal{D}_{m}|\{x_{i}\}\rangle_{0}=\left(\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{|A|}}\right)^{L}\sum_{\{x_{i}^{\prime}\}}\prod_{i=1}^{L}\chi(x_{i}^{-1}x_{i+1},x_{i}^{\prime})|\{x_{i}^{\prime}\}\rangle_{0}.}

(5.13)

We now compute
\mathsf{D}_{m}^{2}
directly.

\displaystyle\mathsf{D}_{m}^{2}|\{x_{i}\}\rangle_{0}

\displaystyle=\left(\frac{1}{|A|}\right)^{L}\sum_{\{x_{i}^{\prime},x_{i}^{\prime\prime}\}}\prod_{i}\chi(x_{i}^{-1}x_{i+1},x_{i}^{\prime})\chi(x_{i}^{\prime-1}x_{i+1}^{\prime},x_{i}^{\prime\prime})|\{x_{i}^{\prime\prime}\}\rangle_{0}

(5.14)

\displaystyle=\left(\frac{1}{|A|}\right)^{L}\sum_{\{x_{i}^{\prime},x_{i}^{\prime\prime}\}}\prod_{i}\chi(x_{i}^{-1}x_{i+1},x_{i}^{\prime})\chi(x_{i}^{\prime},x_{i}^{\prime\prime})^{-1}\chi(x_{i}^{\prime},x_{i-1}^{\prime\prime})|\{x_{i}^{\prime\prime}\}\rangle_{0}.

(5.15)

\displaystyle=\left(\frac{1}{|A|}\right)^{L}\sum_{\{x_{i}^{\prime},x_{i}^{\prime\prime}\}}\prod_{i}\chi(x_{i}^{-1}x_{i+1}x_{i}^{\prime\prime-1}x_{i-1}^{\prime\prime},x_{i}^{\prime})|\{x_{i}^{\prime\prime}\}\rangle_{0}.

(5.16)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\{x_{i}^{\prime\prime}\}}\prod_{i}\delta_{x_{i}^{-1}x_{i+1}x_{i}^{\prime\prime-1}x_{i-1}^{\prime\prime},1}|\{x_{i}^{\prime\prime}\}\rangle_{0},

(5.17)

where in the last step we used
\sum_{a\in A}\chi(a,b)=|A|\delta_{b,1}
. Now observe that the delta symbols impose

x_{i}^{-1}x_{i-1}^{\prime\prime}=x_{i+1}^{-1}x_{i}^{\prime\prime}.

(5.18)

Hence
y:=x_{i}^{-1}x_{i-1}^{\prime\prime}
is independent of
i
. Therefore we have

\displaystyle\mathsf{D}_{m}^{2}|\{x_{i}\}\rangle_{0}

\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in A}\sum_{\{x_{i}^{\prime\prime}\}}\prod_{i}\delta_{x_{i-1}^{\prime\prime},x_{i}y}|\{x_{i}^{\prime\prime}\}\rangle_{0}

(5.19)

\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in A}|yx_{2},yx_{3},\cdots,yx_{L},yx_{1}\rangle_{0}=T\sum_{y\in A}\mathsf{D}_{y}|\{x_{i}\}\rangle_{0},

(5.20)

where
T
is translation by one site to the left. We conclude

\mathsf{D}_{m}^{2}=T\sum_{y\in A}\mathsf{D}_{y}.

(5.21)

Here
\mathrm{ind}(T)=|A|^{-1}
. We can obtain a canonical QCA-refined realization by redefining
\widetilde{\mathsf{D}}_{m}=\mathsf{D}_{m}T^{-1}
. We note that the QCA-refined fusion rules
Equation

5.21
can also be derived diagrammatically as in
Figure

5
.

Appendix A
Conventions

All fusion categories are defined over
\mathbb{C}
and are assumed to be unitary
[
61
]
. For a fusion category
\mathcal{C}
, we write
x\in\mathcal{C}
to mean
x
is an object of
\mathcal{C}
and
x\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C})
to mean
x
is a simple object of
\mathcal{C}
. For
x\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C})
and
n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
we will write
nx
to mean
n
-fold direct sum of
x
. The quantum dimension of an object
x\in\mathcal{C}
is denoted as
d_{x}
. For two objects
x,y\in\mathcal{C}
, we will sometimes abuse notation and write
x=y
to mean that
x
is isomorphic to
y
with an isomorphism chosen. For a general object
X=\oplus_{a\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C})}n_{a}a
there are projection and inclusion morphisms

p_{a}^{\mu}:X\to a,~\ i_{a}^{\mu}:a\to X,~\ \mu=1,\cdots,n_{a},

(A.1)

corresponding to the
\mu
-th copy of
a
in
X
. The unitary structure on the fusion category is defined as
i^{\mu}_{a}=(p_{a}^{\mu})^{\dagger}
, and the inclusions/projections are taken to be orthonormal:
\langle i_{a}^{\mu},i_{a}^{\nu}\rangle=\langle p_{a}^{\mu},p_{a}^{\nu}\rangle=\delta_{\mu,\nu}
.
The concrete examples of fusion categories that we will consider in this paper are all multiplicity-free. We use projection/inclusion basis for fusion/splitting spaces: For simples
a,b,c\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathcal{C})
, trivalent vertices below are understood as the unique projection/inclusion
p_{c}:a\otimes b\to c
and
i_{c}:c\to a\otimes b
.

(A.2)

Other types of morphisms will be defined explicitly and are represented as dots or boxes. The
F
-symbols follow the following convention:
